questions.prompt: Which crusade ended with the sacking of Constantinople rather than reaching Jerusalem?
questions.fact: Venice had financed the fleet and redirected it to settle debts, so the largest Christian city in the world was sacked by a Christian army.

questions.prompt: Which sultan retook Jerusalem from the crusader states in 1187?
questions.fact: He let the defeated inhabitants ransom themselves and quietly paid for many of the poorest, which is why European chroniclers wrote of him admiringly.

questions.prompt: Which Indian emperor renounced warfare after the bloody conquest of Kalinga?
questions.fact: His edicts, carved onto pillars across the subcontinent, are among the oldest deciphered writing in India and read as public apologies.

questions.prompt: Which Korean king commissioned the creation of the Hangul alphabet?
questions.fact: The script was designed so an ordinary labourer could learn it in a morning, which the scholarly elite of the time deeply resented.

questions.prompt: The House of Wisdom, a celebrated centre of translation and scholarship, stood in which city?
questions.fact: Greek works that survive today often do so because they were translated into Arabic there and only much later rendered back into Latin.

questions.prompt: Which Iberian city was the capital of the Umayyad caliphate in Al-Andalus?
questions.fact: At its tenth-century peak it may have been the largest city in Europe, with street lighting and public libraries centuries before its northern rivals.

questions.prompt: Which Persian king is credited in the Hebrew Bible with letting exiled Jews return home?
questions.fact: A clay cylinder recording his treatment of conquered peoples is sometimes called an early charter of rights, though it was standard royal propaganda.

questions.prompt: The Royal Road, a courier highway running some 2,500 kilometres, was built by which empire?
questions.fact: Mounted relay riders could cover it in about a week, a speed Herodotus found astonishing enough to describe in detail.

questions.prompt: Which Mesoamerican city was already an abandoned ruin when the Aztecs named its main avenue?
questions.fact: The Aztecs called it the place where the gods were born. Nobody knows what its own builders called it, or what language they spoke.

questions.prompt: Which early Mesoamerican culture carved colossal stone heads from basalt?
questions.fact: The basalt was hauled dozens of miles from volcanic highlands with no wheels and no draught animals.

questions.prompt: The Kalmar Union of 1397 joined Denmark, Sweden and which other kingdom under one monarch?
questions.fact: It was assembled by Margaret I, who governed three kingdoms without ever formally being crowned queen of any of them.

questions.prompt: Which trading company is generally credited with issuing the world's first publicly traded shares?
questions.fact: It also sold bonds to the general public, and Amsterdam's exchange grew up around people reselling both second-hand.

questions.prompt: Which Russian ruler was the first to be crowned tsar of all Russia, in 1547?
questions.fact: The epithet attached to him translates closer to formidable or awe-inspiring than to wicked, though his later reign earned the harsher reading.

questions.prompt: Which empress expanded Russia to the Black Sea after taking power from her own husband?
questions.fact: She was German by birth with no Romanov blood, which made her lavish patronage of Russian art and law a deliberate act of legitimacy.

questions.prompt: A potato blight beginning in 1845 caused mass death and emigration in which country?
questions.fact: Food kept being exported throughout, which is why the period is remembered less as a crop failure than as a political one.

questions.prompt: Which 1916 rebellion was launched from the General Post Office in Dublin?
questions.fact: It was unpopular while it happened. The executions of its leaders over the following weeks did far more for the cause than the rebellion itself.

questions.prompt: Which volunteer expedition of 1860 advanced Italian unification by landing in Sicily?
questions.fact: Giuseppe Garibaldi handed the conquered south to a king he did not much admire, then retired to farm a small island.

questions.prompt: Which 1381 English uprising was triggered by a poll tax and led in part by Wat Tyler?
questions.fact: The rebels reached London and met the fourteen-year-old king in person. He promised reforms and revoked every one of them within weeks.

questions.prompt: For most of the 14th century the popes resided not in Rome but in which French city?
questions.fact: Seven popes ruled from there in succession, and the eventual return to Rome triggered a schism with rival claimants for another forty years.

questions.prompt: Which US constitutional amendment banned the manufacture and sale of alcohol?
questions.fact: It is the only amendment ever repealed, undone thirteen years later by the one that immediately followed it.

questions.prompt: Which New Deal programme put unemployed young men to work planting trees and building parks?
questions.fact: It planted roughly three billion trees in nine years, and much of the trail and shelter infrastructure in US national parks still dates from it.

questions.prompt: Which 1803 Supreme Court case established the power of US courts to strike down laws?
questions.fact: The court claimed the principle while declining to grant the plaintiff what he had asked for, which left the ruling almost impossible to appeal.

questions.prompt: The first women's rights convention in the United States was held in 1848 in which state?
questions.fact: Its declaration deliberately copied the wording of the Declaration of Independence, with two words added: and women.

questions.prompt: Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968 to end a period of liberalisation known as what?
questions.fact: Its slogan was socialism with a human face. The reversal imposed afterwards was officially called normalisation.

questions.prompt: Which independent trade union emerged from a 1980 strike at the Gdansk shipyard?
questions.fact: It became the first legally recognised free union in a Warsaw Pact country, and nine years later formed the bloc's first non-communist government.

questions.prompt: Which military alliance was formed in 1955 as the Eastern bloc's answer to NATO?
questions.fact: It was signed months after West Germany joined NATO, and its only joint military operation was against one of its own members.

questions.prompt: Which battle of 732 halted Umayyad expansion into Frankish territory?
questions.fact: The victory earned Charles Martel the nickname the Hammer, and gave his grandson Charlemagne the platform for an empire.

questions.prompt: Which sixth-century legal compilation became the foundation of civil law across much of Europe?
questions.fact: Rediscovered in Italian universities five centuries later, it handed medieval lawyers an entire working legal system to argue from.

questions.prompt: Which Egyptian ruler was shown in statues wearing a pharaoh's false beard despite being a woman?
questions.fact: Her successor had her name chiselled off monuments, which is why her twenty-year reign was only reconstructed in the nineteenth century.

questions.prompt: Which West African ruler's 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca reportedly wrecked Egypt's gold price?
questions.fact: He gave away so much gold passing through Cairo that its value there was still depressed a decade later.

questions.prompt: Which effect explains why a siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it leaves?
questions.fact: The same shift in light lets astronomers measure how fast a distant galaxy is moving away from us.

questions.prompt: Which principle states that a faster-moving fluid exerts lower pressure?
questions.fact: It is often credited with lift on a wing, though the full explanation needs the downward deflection of air as well.

questions.prompt: Which quantity always increases in an isolated system, according to the second law of thermodynamics?
questions.fact: It is the reason a broken cup never reassembles: the laws of motion allow it, but the number of disordered arrangements overwhelms the ordered ones.

questions.prompt: What name is given to the supercontinent that began breaking apart around 175 million years ago?
questions.fact: Matching rock formations and fossils on facing Atlantic coastlines were the first clues, decades before anyone could explain what moved them.

questions.prompt: Which layer of the Earth lies directly beneath the crust?
questions.fact: It is solid rock, but over geological timescales it flows slowly enough to drag the plates above it.

questions.prompt: Which region beyond Neptune contains Pluto and many other icy bodies?
questions.fact: Finding other objects of similar size there is what led astronomers to redefine what counts as a planet.

questions.prompt: Which method finds exoplanets by measuring a star's slight dimming?
questions.fact: The dip is often less than one percent of the star's light, which is why the technique needed space telescopes to work reliably.

questions.prompt: Which faint radiation left over from the early universe was detected accidentally in 1965?
questions.fact: The two engineers who found it first blamed pigeon droppings in their antenna, and cleaned it out before accepting the signal was real.

questions.prompt: Which group of the periodic table is famously almost unreactive?
questions.fact: Their outer electron shells are already full, so there is nothing to gain by bonding. A few heavier ones can be forced into compounds anyway.

questions.prompt: Which single-layer form of carbon was isolated in 2004 using adhesive tape?
questions.fact: It is about two hundred times stronger than steel by weight, and the isolation technique was simple enough to repeat in a school lab.

questions.prompt: Which type of cell division produces sex cells with half the usual chromosome count?
questions.fact: Chromosomes swap segments part-way through, which is why siblings differ despite drawing from the same two parents.

questions.prompt: Which gene-editing tool is adapted from a bacterial defence against viruses?
questions.fact: Bacteria store snippets of viral DNA as a memory of past infections, and the editing tool borrows the enzyme that acts on those snippets.

questions.prompt: Which misfolded protein causes diseases such as scrapie and BSE?
questions.fact: It carries no genetic material at all. It spreads by forcing normal proteins to adopt its own shape, which is why heat and radiation do not destroy it.

questions.prompt: Which microscopic animal can survive vacuum, radiation and near-absolute-zero temperatures?
questions.fact: It survives by expelling almost all its water and suspending its metabolism, a state it can hold for years before rehydrating.

questions.prompt: Which sense do sharks use to detect the faint electric fields of hidden prey?
questions.fact: The jelly-filled pores that do the sensing cluster around the snout, which is why a shark can find a fish buried in sand.

questions.prompt: Which whale has a long spiral tusk that is in fact an overgrown tooth?
questions.fact: The tusk is packed with nerve endings and appears to sense water salinity, making it less a weapon than an instrument.

questions.prompt: Which apparent force deflects moving air and water because the Earth is rotating?
questions.fact: It sets the direction storms spin, which is opposite in the two hemispheres. It is far too weak to affect a draining bath.

questions.prompt: Which periodic warming of the eastern Pacific disrupts weather worldwide?
questions.fact: Peruvian fishermen named it after the Christ child because the warm water usually arrived around Christmas.

questions.prompt: Which dating technique measures the decay of an unstable carbon isotope?
questions.fact: It only works back about 50,000 years. Beyond that too little of the isotope remains to measure against the background.

questions.prompt: Which substance is thought to make up most of the universe's matter yet has never been directly detected?
questions.fact: It was inferred because galaxies spin too fast to hold together on their visible mass alone, and would have flung themselves apart long ago.

questions.prompt: Above which temperature does a magnetic material lose its permanent magnetism?
questions.fact: Heat randomises the aligned magnetic domains. Cooling the metal does not restore the alignment on its own.

questions.prompt: Which phenomenon lets certain materials conduct electricity with zero resistance when cooled?
questions.fact: Such a material also expels magnetic fields from its interior, which is what makes the floating-magnet demonstration possible.

questions.prompt: Which copper-based molecule carries oxygen in crabs and octopuses instead of haemoglobin?
questions.fact: Copper turns blue when it binds oxygen rather than red, which is why the blood of a live lobster is faintly blue.

questions.prompt: What is the standard term for a trial in which neither the patient nor the doctor knows who received treatment?
questions.fact: Keeping the doctor in the dark matters as much as the patient, because expectation leaks into how symptoms get recorded.

questions.prompt: Which constant gives the number of particles in one mole of a substance?
questions.fact: It is roughly six followed by twenty-three zeros, chosen so that atomic mass in grams matches the mass of that many atoms.

questions.prompt: Which ocean circulation is driven by differences in water temperature and salinity?
questions.fact: A single parcel of water can take around a thousand years to complete the full loop between the surface and the deep ocean.

questions.prompt: Which type of rock is formed from compressed layers of sediment?
questions.fact: It is the only rock type that routinely preserves fossils, because the other two involve heat that would destroy them.

questions.prompt: Which measurement scale describes how bright a star appears from Earth?
questions.fact: The scale runs backwards, so a lower number means a brighter object, an inheritance from Greek astronomers ranking stars by eye.

questions.prompt: Which process do some bacteria use to convert atmospheric nitrogen into usable compounds?
questions.fact: Legumes host these bacteria in root nodules, which is why crop rotation with beans and clover restores exhausted soil.

questions.prompt: Which particle passes through ordinary matter so easily that trillions cross a person each second?
questions.fact: Detectors are buried deep underground and filled with thousands of tonnes of fluid, all to catch a handful of interactions a day.

questions.prompt: Which gymnast recorded the first perfect ten in Olympic competition, at Montreal in 1976?
questions.fact: The scoreboard could not display four digits and showed 1.00 instead, because nobody had built it expecting the score to be reached.

questions.prompt: Which athlete broke the four-minute mile in 1954?
questions.fact: He was a medical student training in his lunch breaks, and his record lasted just 46 days before a rival beat it.

questions.prompt: Which long jumper's 1968 Olympic mark stood as the world record for 23 years?
questions.fact: The jump exceeded the optical measuring device's range, so officials had to find a tape measure while the crowd waited.

questions.prompt: Which sprinter won three golds at the 1960 Rome Olympics after contracting polio as a child?
questions.fact: She had worn a leg brace until she was nine, and insisted her homecoming parade be the first integrated public event in her Tennessee town.

questions.prompt: Which 1973 tennis match was billed as the Battle of the Sexes?
questions.fact: Around 90 million people watched worldwide, and the winner used the platform to press for equal prize money at the US Open.

questions.prompt: Which swimmer won eight gold medals at a single Olympic Games in 2008?
questions.fact: One of the eight was won by a hundredth of a second, on a final stroke that officials had to review frame by frame.

questions.prompt: Which nation's amateur ice hockey team beat the Soviet Union in the 1980 Winter Olympics?
questions.fact: The Soviets had won every Olympic title since 1964. The winning team still had to beat Finland afterwards to actually take gold.

questions.prompt: Which footballer scored both the Hand of God and the Goal of the Century in the same 1986 match?
questions.fact: The two goals came four minutes apart in the same quarter-final, one an undetected handball and the other a run past five defenders.

questions.prompt: Which club won the Premier League in 2016 having begun the season at 5000 to 1?
questions.fact: Bookmakers had offered the same odds that year on the Loch Ness monster being found, and paid out around 25 million pounds.

questions.prompt: Which basketball player scored 100 points in a single NBA game in 1962?
questions.fact: No footage of the game survives and only 4,124 people attended, so the record exists almost entirely through newspaper accounts.

questions.prompt: Which player broke Babe Ruth's career home run record in 1974?
questions.fact: He received sacks of hate mail and death threats through the chase, and kept the letters for the rest of his life.

questions.prompt: Which player broke Major League Baseball's colour barrier in 1947?
questions.fact: His number is retired across every team in the league, the only player honoured that way.

questions.prompt: Which cricketer finished a Test career with a batting average of 99.94?
questions.fact: Four runs in his final innings would have carried him to 100. He was bowled second ball for nothing.

questions.prompt: Which batter scored one hundred international centuries across a career ending in 2013?
questions.fact: He made his international debut at sixteen against a bowling attack that had already broken his nose by the second Test.

questions.prompt: Which fly-half kicked the drop goal that won the 2003 Rugby World Cup final?
questions.fact: He kicked it with his weaker foot, 26 seconds from the end of extra time, having missed three earlier attempts in the same match.

questions.prompt: Which Formula One driver died at Imola in 1994, prompting a sweeping safety overhaul?
questions.fact: No driver died at a Formula One race weekend for the next twenty years, and his own foundation has since funded schooling for millions of children.

questions.prompt: Which cyclist won all three Grand Tours in the same calendar year, in 1974?
questions.fact: His nickname was the Cannibal, given to him by a rival's daughter because he left nothing for anyone else.

questions.prompt: Which runner covered the marathon distance in under two hours at a 2019 exhibition event in Vienna?
questions.fact: Pacemakers rotated in a V formation and the route was closed and flat, so the time stands as a feat rather than a record.

questions.prompt: Which golfer holds the record for most professional major championships won?
questions.fact: He also finished runner-up in majors nineteen times, more often than anyone else has won them.

questions.prompt: Which boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman took place in Kinshasa in 1974?
questions.fact: The challenger spent seven rounds absorbing punches against the ropes to drain his opponent, a tactic later called rope-a-dope.

questions.prompt: Which American won the world chess championship in Reykjavik in 1972?
questions.fact: He forfeited the second game in a dispute over cameras, then won from a point down against an opponent his federation had prepared for years.

questions.prompt: What is the highest rank a sumo wrestler can attain?
questions.fact: Nobody at that rank can be demoted for losing. A wrestler who stops winning is expected to retire instead.

questions.prompt: Which English hospital's 1948 games for injured veterans grew into the Paralympics?
questions.fact: They were deliberately staged on the opening day of the London Olympics, by a neurologist who treated sport as spinal rehabilitation.

questions.prompt: Which city hosted the 1968 Summer Olympics, where thin air helped shatter sprint records?
questions.fact: At 2,240 metres the air resistance drop favoured sprints and jumps, but distance runners suffered badly in the same conditions.

questions.prompt: Which team won the 2019 Cricket World Cup final on a boundary countback?
questions.fact: The match and the super over both finished level, so the title went to whoever had hit more boundaries. The rule was scrapped afterwards.

questions.prompt: Which team won the first Super Bowl, played in January 1967?
questions.fact: The game did not sell out, and the only surviving broadcast tape was recorded off television by a fan at home.

questions.prompt: Which physical education instructor invented basketball in 1891 using two peach baskets?
questions.fact: The bottoms of the baskets were left in at first, so someone had to fetch the ball down with a ladder after every score.

questions.prompt: In Formula One, what does the drag reduction system do to a car's rear wing?
options: Opens a flap on the straights
questions.fact: It can only be used within a second of the car ahead at set points on the track, so it aids overtaking without helping a leader escape.

questions.prompt: Which two sports joined the Olympic programme for the first time at the delayed Tokyo Games?
questions.fact: The skateboarding gold medallists in the women's park event were 19, 12 and 16 years old.

questions.prompt: Which footballer has won the most Ballon d'Or awards?
questions.fact: The award was restricted to European players until 1995, so several earlier South American greats were never eligible for it at all.

questions.prompt: Which animated film about two children in wartime Japan was directed by Isao Takahata?
questions.fact: It was released as a double bill with My Neighbour Totoro, which sent audiences home from one of the gentlest films ever made and one of the bleakest.

questions.prompt: Which manga and anime series is set in a walled city besieged by giant humanoids?
questions.fact: Its author drew the first chapter after a customer at the internet cafe where he worked cornered him, and he could not get away.

questions.prompt: Which video game is the best-selling of all time, with over 300 million copies sold?
questions.fact: It was bought by Microsoft for 2.5 billion dollars from a studio that had fewer than fifty employees at the time.

questions.prompt: Which studio developed the video game series about the monster hunter Geralt of Rivia?
questions.fact: The studio began as a company importing and translating foreign games for the Polish market, because piracy made selling them any other way impossible.

questions.prompt: Which pink spherical Nintendo character copies the abilities of enemies he swallows?
questions.fact: He was originally a placeholder shape the designer intended to replace, and the team liked him enough to keep him.

questions.prompt: Which film won seven Academy Awards in 2023 including Best Picture?
questions.fact: Its lead actress became the first Asian woman to win Best Actress, forty years into a career that Hollywood had mostly cast as scenery.

questions.prompt: Which comedian wrote and directed the 2017 horror film Get Out?
questions.fact: He wrote it partly to argue that racism had not ended, and shelved it repeatedly believing nobody would finance it.

questions.prompt: Which South Korean director made the first non-English film to win Best Picture?
questions.fact: He told the audience at an earlier ceremony that subtitles are a one-inch barrier, and won four Oscars weeks later.

questions.prompt: Which actor played the title role in the 2018 film Black Panther?
questions.fact: He filmed the role while undergoing treatment for an illness he told almost nobody about, including most of the cast.

questions.prompt: Which musical set among struggling New York artists features the song Seasons of Love?
questions.fact: Its writer died of an aortic aneurysm the night before the first public performance, aged 35.

questions.prompt: Which artist painted the 1937 mural protesting the bombing of a Basque town?
questions.fact: A tapestry copy hangs at the United Nations, and was covered over in 2003 during a press conference about invading Iraq.

questions.prompt: Which Japanese artist is known for polka dots and mirrored infinity rooms?
questions.fact: She has lived voluntarily in a psychiatric hospital since 1977, walking to her studio across the street to work every day.

questions.prompt: Which anonymous street artist created the stencil work Girl with Balloon?
questions.fact: A framed copy shredded itself at auction seconds after selling. The half-destroyed version resold three years later for eighteen times the price.

questions.prompt: Which singer released the surprise pandemic album Folklore in 2020?
questions.fact: It was announced sixteen hours before release, breaking an industry habit of months-long promotional campaigns.

questions.prompt: Which rapper released the 2015 album To Pimp a Butterfly?
questions.fact: He later became the first artist outside jazz or classical music to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music.

questions.prompt: Which South Korean girl group released the single How You Like That in 2020?
questions.fact: They became the first Korean girl group to headline Coachella, three years after the pandemic postponed their original slot.

questions.prompt: Which Spanish series follows robbers in red jumpsuits occupying the Royal Mint?
questions.fact: It was cancelled after a poor domestic run, then bought by a streaming service, recut into shorter episodes and became a global hit.

questions.prompt: Which television series follows the Roy family's fight over a media conglomerate?
questions.fact: Its theme was written to sound like a grand orchestral piece played slightly wrong, mirroring a family with money but no dignity.

questions.prompt: Which toy line features robots that convert into vehicles?
questions.fact: The toys existed first as two unrelated Japanese lines, and the whole mythology was written afterwards to connect them.

questions.prompt: Which board game involves building settlements and trading wood, brick and ore?
questions.fact: Its designer was a dental technician who developed it over five years at his kitchen table, testing it on his family.

questions.prompt: Which theme park opened in Anaheim, California in 1955?
questions.fact: The opening day was a disaster of counterfeit tickets, melting asphalt and broken water fountains, later known internally as Black Sunday.

questions.prompt: Which site ranks posts by up and down votes within communities run by volunteer moderators?
questions.fact: Its founders seeded the early site with fake accounts posting to each other, so it would not look empty to real arrivals.

questions.prompt: Which animated series follows a washed-up sitcom star who is also a horse?
questions.fact: Its first six episodes were widely dismissed as an animal-pun comedy, which the writers had built deliberately as a setup.

questions.prompt: Which designer introduced the New Look silhouette in 1947?
questions.fact: The full skirts used up to twenty metres of fabric, which drew protests in countries still under wartime rationing.

questions.prompt: Which film features a fictional theme park where cloned dinosaurs escape their enclosures?
questions.fact: Most of the dinosaurs on screen are animatronic. Only about six minutes of the film uses computer-generated creatures.

questions.prompt: Which singing competition format has judges facing away until they hear a voice they like?
questions.fact: The turning chair was designed to stop judges picking on looks, and the format was created in the Netherlands before selling to 145 countries.

questions.prompt: Which musician performed a rooftop concert on Savile Row in London in January 1969?
questions.fact: Police shut it down after 42 minutes, and it was the group's final public performance together.

questions.prompt: Which film series features a resistance fighter named Furiosa in a desert wasteland?
questions.fact: The 2015 entry used around 150 practical vehicles built for the shoot, and filmed most of its chases in the Namib desert.

questions.prompt: Which comic strip features a boy and his imaginary tiger?
questions.fact: Its creator refused all merchandising and retired the strip after ten years, which is why almost every tiger sticker you see is unlicensed.

questions.prompt: Which annual festival takes place at Worthy Farm in Somerset?
questions.fact: It began in 1970 charging one pound including free milk from the farm, and drew about 1,500 people.

questions.prompt: Which country is crossed by both the equator and the Tropic of Capricorn?
questions.fact: Only two countries are crossed by both lines. The other is on the opposite side of the Atlantic.

questions.prompt: Which country gained independence in 2011, making it the world's newest UN member?
questions.fact: It voted to separate by almost 99 percent, and slid into civil war within two years of the result.

questions.prompt: Kaliningrad is an exclave of which country?
questions.fact: It was the German city of Konigsberg until 1945, and is now separated from its own country by two EU members.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest landlocked country in the world by area?
questions.fact: It is bigger than all of Western Europe, and its access to the Caspian does not count because that sea has no outlet to an ocean.

questions.prompt: Which European microstate is doubly landlocked, surrounded only by landlocked neighbours?
questions.fact: Only one other country in the world shares this position, and it sits in Central Asia.

questions.prompt: Which territory's capital is Iqaluit?
questions.fact: It was carved out of the Northwest Territories in 1999, and no road connects its capital to the rest of the country.

questions.prompt: Which Australian state has Brisbane as its capital?
questions.fact: It is the only mainland state that does not observe daylight saving, having rejected it in a referendum in 1992.

questions.prompt: Which US state has Frankfort as its capital?
questions.fact: The capital is the fifth-smallest in the country by population, and was chosen as a compromise between two rival cities.

questions.prompt: Which strait separates the northern tip of Australia from Papua New Guinea?
questions.fact: At its narrowest the gap is about 150 kilometres, and it was a land bridge as recently as 8,000 years ago.

questions.prompt: Which strait is the narrowest crossing of the English Channel?
questions.fact: It is about 33 kilometres across, which is why the Channel Tunnel and every swimming record follow the same line.

questions.prompt: Which inland sea shrank drastically after Soviet irrigation diverted its feeder rivers?
questions.fact: Fishing boats now sit on dry salt flats dozens of kilometres from any water, and the exposed seabed generates toxic dust storms.

questions.prompt: Which African lake bordered by four countries has lost most of its surface area since the 1960s?
questions.fact: It has shrunk by around 90 percent, and the resulting competition for water is a driver of conflict across the Sahel.

questions.prompt: Which peninsula makes up the mainland of Denmark?
questions.fact: It is the only part of the country attached to continental Europe. The rest is more than 400 islands.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest island in Europe?
questions.fact: It is ninth-largest in the world, and is one of the few large islands whose name refers to size rather than to a people.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest island in the world?
questions.fact: Australia is bigger but counts as a continental landmass, which is the only reason this one holds the title.

questions.prompt: Which mountain range runs along the border of Norway and Sweden?
questions.fact: The range is old and heavily eroded, which is why its peaks are modest but its glacial valleys are so deep they flooded into fjords.

questions.prompt: Which southern African country has Portuguese as its official language?
questions.fact: It is the only country whose flag features a modern rifle, a relic of the independence war fought against the colonial power.

questions.prompt: Which country has the only national flag that is not a rectangle?
questions.fact: It is two stacked pennants, and its exact geometry is specified in the constitution as a set of construction instructions.

questions.prompt: Which is the smallest sovereign state in the world by area?
questions.fact: At about 49 hectares it is smaller than many city parks, and it has no hospital, so nobody is officially born there.

questions.prompt: Which US city is nicknamed the Motor City?
questions.fact: It is the only US city to have declared the largest municipal bankruptcy in the country's history, in 2013.

questions.prompt: Which country contains the vast salt flat known as the Salar de Uyuni?
questions.fact: When a thin layer of water sits on it the flat becomes a near-perfect mirror, and satellites use it to calibrate their instruments.

questions.prompt: Which country contains the granite towers of Torres del Paine?
questions.fact: The park sits in Patagonia, where winds regularly exceed 100 kilometres per hour and blow lake spray uphill.

questions.prompt: Which country contains the temple plain of Bagan?
questions.fact: More than 2,000 brick temples still stand across the plain, out of an estimated 10,000 built between the 11th and 13th centuries.

questions.prompt: Which line of latitude marks the northern edge of the tropics?
questions.fact: It moves. The Earth's tilt wobbles slightly, so the line drifts about 15 metres closer to the equator each year.

questions.prompt: Which country has the most pyramids in the world?
questions.fact: The Nubian kingdoms built around twice as many as their northern neighbour, though theirs are smaller and much more steeply angled.

questions.prompt: Which sea's name literally means the middle of the land?
questions.fact: It loses more water to evaporation than its rivers supply, so it is refilled by a constant inward current through a narrow western strait.

questions.prompt: Which country is the world's largest producer of palm oil?
questions.fact: The crop yields several times more oil per hectare than any alternative, which is exactly why the pressure on rainforest is so intense.

questions.prompt: Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
questions.fact: It is the only country in the world lying entirely above 1,000 metres, which is why it fields a competitive distance-running team.

questions.prompt: Which country contains the Rub al Khali, the world's largest continuous sand desert?
questions.fact: Its name translates as the empty quarter. Dunes there reach 250 metres, and parts had no recorded crossing until the 1930s.

questions.prompt: Which country's territory includes the island of Svalbard?
questions.fact: A 1920 treaty lets citizens of over 40 countries live and work there without a visa, which is why it has a Russian mining settlement.

questions.prompt: Which crime novel introduced the hacker Lisbeth Salander?
options: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
questions.fact: Its author delivered three manuscripts and died of a heart attack before the first was published, never seeing a single copy sell.

questions.prompt: Which novel is set around a Barcelona library called the Cemetery of Forgotten Books?
questions.fact: It has sold more than 15 million copies, making its author the most widely read Spanish novelist after Cervantes.

questions.prompt: Which eleventh-century Japanese work is often called the world's first novel?
questions.fact: It was written by a lady of the imperial court, in a script then considered women's writing because men wrote in Chinese.

questions.prompt: Which Chinese classical novel follows a monk and a rebellious monkey on a pilgrimage?
questions.fact: The monkey's story has been adapted so often that he is probably the most filmed character in the world.

questions.prompt: Which Sanskrit epic follows a prince's exile and the rescue of his abducted wife?
questions.fact: It is still performed annually across South and Southeast Asia, in shadow puppetry, dance and now television serials.

questions.prompt: Which Persian mathematician and poet is credited with the Rubaiyat?
questions.fact: He was better known in his lifetime for reforming the calendar and solving cubic equations than for any verse.

questions.prompt: Which novel by Isabel Allende follows the Trueba family across generations in Chile?
